newsitem.title: UK: British unions furious at reported Labour split.
newsitem.headline: British unions furious at reported Labour split.

text.p: British trade unions reacted furiously on Friday to reports the Labour Party was planning to sever its historic links with the unions.
Denials from Labour were only half-believed by union officials who have been appalled by the way the party has sought in recent months to distance itself from its old allies in the labour movement.

Labour leader Tony Blair acted quickly late on Thursday to deny comments attributed to his employment spokesman Stephen Byers that the century-old links would be cut if the unions lead a wave of strikes under a Labour government.
But Lew Adams, leader of rail drivers' union ASLEF, said: "You can't keep kicking the unions in the teeth when we're trying to help the Labour Party become the next government."
A Labour spokesman said: "These stories have no foundation at all. Mr Blair made no such proposal and no such proposal is even under discussion."
Byers claimed he had said nothing during a dinner with political correspondents to justify their "ludicrous" stories.
Exasperated union leaders acknowledged the reports had been denied, but used words like "crass" and "naive" to describe the behaviour of Labour this week.

The conference of the Trades Union Congress (TUC) has been overshadowed by rows over Labour proposals to curb strikes, and the party's lukewarm response to union demands for a national minimum wage and new rights at work has also riled activists.

Officials of the TUC umbrella body are angry that the "New Unionism" of moderate leader John Monks, focused on workplace organisation and partnership with employers, has barely had a mention in the media because of the political row.

"The politics at the edges of conference have been a distraction. The real point for any politican is that unions are popular," Monks said, adding surveys showed Britons felt the Conservative government's "union-bashing" had gone too far.
"We have been distracted when we've tried to show how reasonable we can be," Adams said, complaining that Labour had "hijacked the conference".
The next election is due within eight months and Labour is well ahead in the polls.

Blair has diluted union influence on the party, but unions still provide half the party's funds and have half the votes at its policy conference, and some of Blair's advisers believe the relationship remains an electoral liability.

The government played on these fears, saying the minimum wage of 4.26 pounds ($6.63) an hour demanded by the unions would destroy a million jobs, and denouncing further strikes called by postal and rail unions during the week.
